items.title: Show HN: Phonon TTS on WebGPU, 44MB, 115x real time, with live word timings
items.text:
Show HN: Phonon TTS on WebGPU, 44MB, 115x real time, with live word timings
I tried Gradium's Phonon 31M text-to-speech model and was blown away by its quality to size ratio. I needed timings for every word to be able to highlight them, so I wrote a second runtime for it with a different design: the whole generation loop stays on the GPU in WebGPU kernels written specifically for this by Claude Opus 5.5.When initialized, it can start streaming audio in about 3 ms, and it only needs to download 44 MB (<40 MB brotli'd) instead of the official 67 MB, because every large matrix is stored as int8, the audio decoder included. On the same devices it runs at 115x real time vs. 31x on my M3 Max, and 26x against 13x on my iPhone 17 Pro. The timings are read from one of the model's attention heads while it speaks, so we practically get the time offsets of words for free.Demo

items.title: Show HN: An Open Source Superhuman Email Client Clone
items.text:
Show HN: An Open Source Superhuman Email Client Clone
Hi HN, I'm a long-time Superhuman user, and a few weeks ago I cloned it as a native Mac app.It's keyboard-first, with split inboxes, reminders, and a built-in calendar. It's local-first, including the AI features that use local models shipped in macOS 27, with the option to use Claude/Codex subscriptions. It's extremely configurable, even down to the search weights, and comes packed with CLI/MCP if you want to use it with an agent.This is my daily driver for email, but it's by no means a "stable" product. Use at your own risk. I'm also working on a mobile app to go along with it.Enjoy.

items.title: Apollo Is Vastly Outspending the Neoclouds on AI Chips
items.text:
Apollo Is Vastly Outspending the Neoclouds on AI Chips
Last week, SpaceX’s announcement that it would lease $40 billion worth of Nvidia Vera Rubin chips was a further signal of Elon Musk’s grand ambitions in the AI race. The deal also underscores the arrival of a new big player in that competition: Apollo Global Management, a 36-year-old private-equity pioneer turned private-lending giant. In the deal with SpaceX, Apollo will purchase the chips through a subsidiary, then lease them to Musk’s company. The arrangement follows a supersized Apollo deal announced in June, one that also involves Broadcom and Blackstone, another large money management firm: a $35 billion fundraising for Apollo to buy Google’s tensor processing units and lease them to Anthropic.

items.title: Tell HN: Claude Code queries raw GitHub token on startup
items.text:
Tell HN: Claude Code queries raw GitHub token on startup
It's probably known but I was caught off guard yesterday when I noticed that Claude Code (CC) runs `gh auth token --hostname github.com` on every startup which typically returns raw token. e.g. $ gh auth token --hostname github.com gho_0000000000000000000000000000000000000000 I noticed this behaviour by chance when I configured gh to use 1Password for auth[1] and I kept getting prompted by 1Password for authorization repeatedly even when just launching an empty CC session.I don't feel comfortable my GH token being read like that and since I use Nix to manage my system I quickly wrapped `gh auth token ..`[2] to return a fake token and so far nothing breaks.However, I'd be interested to learn why is this behaviour the way its, does anybody have a clue?[1] https://www.1password.dev/cli/shell-

New text: - Added a record of your answer when Claude Code asks to turn on the mods it writes in a session | - Added `assume_role` on `mantle` upstreams of the Claude apps gateway, for a role in another AWS account and for per-developer AWS cost attribution | - Added an `effort` option to a mod's `$.model.fork`, so a quick side job can run at `low` whatever effort the session uses; the result reports the effort sent | - Added the date a stored claude.ai sign-in ends to `claude auth status` (`loginExpiresAt`) and to `claude -p` JSON results (`credential_expires_at`) | - Added a one-line stderr warning to `claude -p` text output, starting 10 days before a stored claude.ai sign-in ends | - Fixed `--continue` sometimes losing the earlier conversation after a malformed tool call's retries ran out (regression in 2.1.314) | - Fixed macOS sessions with many running Bash commands stalling while memory grew | - Fixed permission prompts being answered by keys typed just after sending a message, or before a

new_lines: - Added a record of your answer when Claude Code asks to turn on the mods it writes in a session
- Added `assume_role` on `mantle` upstreams of the Claude apps gateway, for a role in another AWS account and for per-developer AWS cost attribution
- Added an `effort` option to a mod's `$.model.fork`, so a quick side job can run at `low` whatever effort the session uses; the result reports the effort sent
- Added the date a stored claude.ai sign-in ends to `claude auth status` (`loginExpiresAt`) and to `claude -p` JSON results (`credential_expires_at`)
- Added a one-line stderr warning to `claude -p` text output, starting 10 days before a stored claude.ai sign-in ends
- Fixed `--continue` sometimes losing the earlier conversation after a malformed tool call's retries ran out (regression in 2.1.314)
- Fixed macOS sessions with many running Bash commands stalling while memory grew
- Fixed permission prompts being answered by keys typed just after sending a message, or before a slow prompt appeared

- Fixed `/logout`, `claude auth logout` and `claude mcp remove` reporting success, and changes to trust, consent or MCP settings being dropped with no word, when the config file could not be updated on a shared network home directory
- Fixed jobs exiting with `Not logged in` when another terminal or host signs in again to the same account and organization on the same home
- Fixed `claude mcp add` and `remove` writing the config without its lock: they now wait for it or exit 1, though another job's save can still replace a saved server
- Fixed `claude plugin` commands exiting before a slow token refresh was saved, which could sign you out on the next run

items.title: Show HN: Modelpeers – a changelog for the AI models and agents you use
items.text:
Show HN: Modelpeers – a changelog for the AI models and agents you use
Earlier this year, I had one of my product's features down for 48 hours because Anthropic retired Claude 3 Haiku. In another instance, an API parameter started returning errors.I grew sick of not being able to follow and track the endless changes of AI models every week, so I decided to build Modelpeers. It's basically a feed of all these changes. You can follow models and agents that you use to see what is changing and what you need to do about it. Optionally, you can sign up to get a digest for the models/agents you follow.Every few hours, it downloads and hashes dozens of pages from the prominent AI companies' pages, like changelogs, deprecation pages, status pages, and pricing pages. items.text:
Show HN: Uncracked City, detective game where you question LLM suspects that lie
To give you some context on the project. I'm a solo founder and I use AI heavily in my work. The idea came from wanting players to discover cities. Each city has its own history, so every case is set in a real city with real public places. The crime and the people are on other hand invented. The part that I care most is the playable aspect of the game, a model plays the detective and must solve the case before it goes live.As of today: it's free on Android, the iOS version is still waiting to be reviewed by Apple. It's available in six popular languages, but adding more languages is just a matter of time and demand.My long term vision if it takes off: weekly cases, private parties like a team-building escape game, an MCP so a game master can build their own scenario from ChatGPT or Claude,

items.title: Show HN: Kairos – Open-source risk and fraud decisioning platform
items.text:
Show HN: Kairos – Open-source risk and fraud decisioning platform
Hey HN, Ayan here from Finic. We’re launching Kairos, an open source alternative to Sift, Sardine, and other real-time fraud decisioning platforms. Kairos addresses two of the biggest problems facing traditional decisioning tools: a lack of labeled data to train on and dealing with fraudsters that are constantly changing their tactics.1. Traditional fraud solutions use ML models such as XGBoost to detect fraud, but these models are dependent on quality labeled data which many businesses do not have. We address this by using “System One” decision models in additional to traditional models such as XGBoost and logistic regression. items.author: Don't Worry About the Vase (Zvi)
items.title: OpenAI Updates Its Model Spec
items.text:
OpenAI Updates Its Model Spec
The Model Spec is potentially OpenAI’s most important document. It outlines what they aspire for the model to do, and how it should think. I’ve already covered a previous version in depth, so my strategy this time is to look at the diff. I had a Google Doc created for this purpose, and will be working from there. A bunch of things get moved around or reworded, often piecemeal. There are a lot of line edits, most of which are improvements. I’m focusing on what looks new and important. My main new critique is that many of the new examples do not carve reality at its joints, instead having overdetermined answers, and fail to teach the model or reader what the Spec wants them to do in actually difficult cases. Overall I see the new Model Spec as philosophically and practically similar to the old Model Spec. That is not a terrible place to be, as the old Model Spec was a solid document with many strong details. It also means this is a highly ‘optional’ post for those who do not have cause to dig into such weeds. Table of Contents Five Values. Meet the New Spec. New Risk Taxonomy. The Letter and the Spirit. Your Funeral. Context Clues. Preserve User Control

items.title: Claude Code CHANGELOG changed
items.text: Claude Code CHANGELOG changed. New text: - Added a warning to `/schedule` when a new cloud scheduled task gets connectors you did not ask for, with how to remove them | - Added a check that asks before a web or shell tool call sends your account email address to the network | - Added `onFailure: "block"` for Agent SDK hook callbacks, so a callback that fails blocks the action instead of letting it run | - Added a notice in Claude Desktop's Code tab when your organization's remote managed settings haven't loaded for the session, and another once they do | - Added a notice when auto mode's check has no answer for a subagent's tool call, which used to leave nothing in the main view | - Added `anthropic.plan`, `anthropic.seat_type`, `anthropic.provider` and `anthropic.custom_base_url` to OTel metrics, events and spans | - Added a cost report to the Claude apps gateway admin API, `GET /v1/organizations/analytics/cost`, for reading past spend over a date range in total, per developer, per day or per IdP group | - Added a daily reco

new_lines: - Added a warning to `/schedule` when a new cloud scheduled task gets connectors you did not ask for, with how to remove them
- Added a check that asks before a web or shell tool call sends your account email address to the network
- Added `onFailure: "block"` for Agent SDK hook callbacks, so a callback that fails blocks the action instead of letting it run
- Added a notice in Claude Desktop's Code tab when your organization's remote managed settings haven't loaded for the session, and another once they do
- Added a notice when auto mode's check has no answer for a subagent's tool call, which used to leave nothing in the main view
- Added `anthropic.plan`, `anthropic.seat_type`, `anthropic.provider` and `anthropic.custom_base_url` to OTel metrics, events and spans
- Added a cost report to the Claude apps gateway admin API, `GET /v1/organizations/analytics/cost`, for reading past spend over a date range in total, per developer, per day or per IdP group
- Added a daily record of each developer's IdP groups on Claude apps gateways with `admin:` set, kept for `admin.identity_retention_days`, which the cost report groups by
- Added `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NESTED_SESSION_ID`: set it to `1` on a self-hosted runner to have `claude -p` run inside a session use that session's ID and transcript, as in earlier versions
- Fixed project and local MCP servers disconnecting after the first turn in some Claude desktop sessions
- Fixed auto mode failing every turn when an LLM gateway set as the base URL answers 403 or 422 to its server-side safety check (a 403 with an apiKeyHelper is unchanged)
- Fixed `claude auth status` exiting before a slow token refresh was saved, which could sign you out on the next run

Its engineers have found Claude cuts down the time it takes to design chips compared to their estimates of traditional workflows at large chip designers such as Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices, said some of the people.

items.title: [AINews] LLMs can read & write neural network weights: "Weight Space Programming" cuts Autoresearch out of the RSI loop
items.text:
[AINews] LLMs can read & write neural network weights: "Weight Space Programming" cuts Autoresearch out of the RSI loop
Amid a deepening bear market for AI/tech (worthy of dark humor) with Anthropic bonds receiving a “junk” rating and OpenAI fundraise headlines, we continue to see very surprising capability finds in the community, such as today. The best way to put today’s blockbuster paper in context is to recall Karpathy’s autoresearch from a mere 8 months ago, which presaged a summer of recursive self improvement fears: Abstractly, the demonstration is that you can take a sufficiently smart model and through running a series of experiments across a compute cluster, train a model autonomously without human expertise or intervention. However, this is usually done by an involved process of writing PyTorch/Jax code and running compute and watching loss curves and reading evals and optimizing kernels and data and…. Well, last month’s guest Alex Zhang comes back to coauthor a MONSTER discovery: what if you just ask a smart model to directly read and edit the weights of a dumber model? items.title: v0.2.177
items.text:
v0.2.177

### New Features

- **`on_failure` option for `HookMatcher`**: Control what happens when a hook callback fails. Set `on_failure="block"` to block the action when a callback raises, returns `None`, or returns a value the CLI rejects. Defaults to `"continue"` (treat failure as no decision). Requires a CLI version that supports this option; connecting to an older CLI with `on_failure="block"` raises `CLIConnectionError` (#1460)

### Internal/Other Changes

- Updated bundled Claude CLI to version 2.1.317
- Tests: e2e tests now accept either `Bash` or `PowerShell` tool in shell-dependent tests, fixing intermittent failures on Windows (#1467)


---

**PyPI:** https://pypi.org/project/claude-agent-sdk/0.2.177/

```bash
pip install claude-agent-sdk==0.2.177
```

- Added a warning to `/schedule` when a new cloud scheduled task gets connectors you did not ask for, with how to remove them

- Added a notice in Claude Desktop's Code tab when your organization's remote managed settings haven't loaded for the session, and another once they do

llm 0.37
Release: llm 0.37 There's a lot of stuff in this new release of my LLM CLI tool and Python library, representing around two months of accumulated features and fixes. I added gpt-6.1-sol and gpt-6.1-terra, plus a new llm openai endpoint add command to make it easier to configure additional models that use OpenAI-compatible endpoints. I switched the default model (if you have not set your own default) to gpt-6-luna - half the price of the previous default, gpt-5.6-luna. LLM's support for embeddings now accepts that different binary content may have different content-type - necessary for models like Gemini Embedding 2, which can embed text, audio, images, and video. A lot of open source maintainers complain about a flood of AI-assisted PRs. LLM is my project that has been most affected by this and, to be honest, I'm not finding it to be a problem. That's mainly because I have Opus 5.5 or GPT-6 Astra help me with triage to spot the most useful fixes! This release includes fixes from 12 authors - almost all AI-assisted - and the burden of reviewing them wasn't nearly as great as I expected. items.title: Scott Alexander’s Against SURA Seems Deeply Confused
items.text:
Scott Alexander’s Against SURA Seems Deeply Confused
If you are helping build something that might kill everyone, maybe stop doing that. Ideally, when you do stop, tell everyone else to also stop building it. That is certainly the obvious, first-level thing to do. You need a damn good reason to decide that no, actually you should keep building the thing that might kill everyone. Scott Alexander is worried too many people are insisting upon this too loudly. He comes out against a strategy focused on getting people to stop. I disagree. I think many of the claims, arguments and rhetoric in Scott’s post are quite poor by the standards that Scott Alexander would apply to himself. Scott clearly continues to support advocacy for a global pause, or what he calls Plan A. His objection is to those advocating primarily or exclusively for SURA, which stands for ‘stop unilaterally and raise awareness.’ The practical differences here are smaller than they may at first appear. This post first lays out my understanding of Scott Alexander’s core claims, then gives my core reactions to those claims, then goes over various questions in detail along with gathering the resulting discussions. Haiku 5.5 now available on Kiro in AWS GovCloud (US)
A new Anthropic model is now available in the Kiro IDE and CLI for the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. With Haiku 5.5, all three Claude 5.5 models are now available in Kiro in AWS GovCloud (US). Claude Haiku 5.5 is the fastest model in the Claude 5.5 family. It's a clear step up from Claude Haiku 4.5, built for work that runs in large volumes and needs quick responses. Developers can use it to summarize and compact long context, classify and route requests, process text in bulk, and make small, targeted edits across many files. It also works well as a review subagent that runs in parallel, while Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 take on harder planning and coding work. Haiku 5.5 uses adaptive thinking across five effort levels from low to max, with medium as the default. It's available with a 1M context window and a 0.06x credit multiplier. Requests over 100K tokens are billed at a 0.3x multiplier. Ensure your IDE or CLI is updated to the latest version, then restart it to access the new model from the model selector. items.title: Anthropic clamps down on Claude’s AI video game clones
items.text:
Anthropic clamps down on Claude’s AI video game clones
Anthropic has updated Claude Code's system prompt to prevent the AI tool from being used to re-create existing video games, as reported by Tom's Hardware. Retro gaming is currently being overrun with AI-made decompilations, recompilations, and ports, but while Anthropic will still let people use Claude Code to make games, it doesn't want people to use it for direct clones. Last week, a user on X posted a screenshot allegedly showing two new sentences added to Claude Code's system prompt: "Do build original games, games in a genre, and games from the user's own designs and assets. Don't build a recreation of a specific existing game, even if … Read the full story at The Verge.

items.text:
Launch HN: Momentic (YC W24) – Agents that catch bugs by using your app
Hey HN, we’re Wei-Wei and Jeff. We’re building Momentic, QA agents that autonomously plan, explore, and bug-bash controls and user flows in your web, iOS, Android, and (soon) desktop apps to catch bugs.Here’s a demo: https://youtu.be/BFsM-Se1Fh8We’re both software engineers that spent our careers on dev tooling and infra across companies like Robinhood, Retool, WeWork, and Qualtrics. Testing was always a pain in the ass (esp Playwright and Selenium), so we built agents to do it for us.Modern day software has a ton of bugs and the change failure rate is only growing faster as coding agent adoption scales. LLMs are really good at generating code, but reinforce their own assumptions, write a ton of useless tests, and are bad at visual understanding. On DeepSWE v1.1, Sonnet 5.5 hit 66.2% pass

items.title: It’s Contract Renewal Season, But Some Customers Aren’t Biting
items.text:
It’s Contract Renewal Season, But Some Customers Aren’t Biting
My colleagues and I have been hearing a lot of stories about big enterprise customers renegotiating their annual contracts with model developers. Traditionally, software sellers use this time as an opportunity to convince customers to increase their annual commit by, for instance, reminding them how they exceeded their usage limits this year or highlighting new features they’ve released. In the past, model developers have had success using that playbook.This year has been a different story, though, some customers tell me. For instance, one executive at a major financial services firm said their company was hesitant to increase their spending commitment with Anthropic, OpenAI or any other model provider for a couple reasons. First, this executive said, the rapid pace of model releases means enterprises want flexibility to quickly switch to whatever the best new model is, something that can change week to week.

items.text:
Show HN: Nomos – A Go harness that stops coding agents from cheating on tests
Hi HN, Mark here.If you've pointed Claude Code, Cursor, or OpenCode at a codebase you care about and walked away thinking AI coding tools are a net negative, I pretty much agree with you.Left directly on a working branch, models optimize for shutting the compiler up on the current turn. Hit a tricky failure and they delete the failing assertion, return a hardcoded nil/true stub, rewrite the spec to match broken code, dump a 300-line function into the wrong package, or burn $15 of tokens editing in circles. Writing longer rules files ("IMPORTANT: NEVER DELETE TESTS") breaks down once context fills up.Starting over the summer I built Nomos: a single 28MB stripped static Go binary (CGO_ENABLED=0, Apache 2.0) that sits between your repo and whatever coding agent you already use. items.title: The U.S. Census Bureau and “Super Intelligence”
items.text:
The U.S. Census Bureau and “Super Intelligence”
I was reminded today of AI Adoption Rate Trending Down for Large Companies, a chart produced by Apollo Global Management in September 2025, which appeared to show a slowdown in U.S. corporate AI adoption based on numbers collected by the U.S. Census Bureau. At the time I used that chart to demonstrate GPT-5 data analysis, and then to experiment with Claude's new Code Interpreter. I decided to try running those numbers again to see what had changed over the past year, and in doing so learned that the Bureau has fallen foul of Executive Order 14434, aka the asinine Super Intelligence one. First, the updated chart Every two weeks the U.S. Census Bureau runs a survey called the Business Trends and Outlook Survey (aka BTOS). Each time it goes to 200,000 businesses out of 1.2 million total - the surveyed group (a "panel") cycles such that an individual business only completes the survey every twelve weeks. The latest data is published on alternating Thursdays at 10am. items.author: SemiAnalysis
items.title: GDPx: Measuring Frontier Model Capabilities Across the Most Valuable Domains
items.text:
GDPx: Measuring Frontier Model Capabilities Across the Most Valuable Domains
GDPx is a benchmark that covers the most valuable domains for frontier intelligence. It aims to be the world’s best benchmark for measuring general agentic capabilities.We believe the first trillion dollars of AI revenue will be concentrated in sectors that can deploy frontier intelligence at high ROI, not broadly diffused throughout the whole economy. Building a general-purpose benchmark based on share of GDP or the SOC/O*NET occupational taxonomy is therefore a mistake. If your goal is to track the progress of frontier models, you should focus on the domains where they will be most impactful.Specifically, we cover the following domains:Chip designCybersecurityBiologyFinanceLegalQuant tradingRecursive self-improvement (RSI)Hardware designMaterials scienceAlignmentSoftware engineeringAnd intentionally forgo industries like government, real estate, and insurance.Interpreting the resultsGDPx is a true frontier-level benchmark: even the best model scores just 12%.Source: GDPxIt’s worth emphasizing that certain models like Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra have sandbagged overall scores due to their safety classifiers.

items.title: The Information’s WTF Summit in Pictures
items.text:
The Information’s WTF Summit in Pictures
At The Information’s annual WTF Summit a few days ago, women leaders from Anthropic, Google, Goldman Sachs and dozens of other companies across technology and media gathered to discuss the forces remaking those industries. Conversation topics ranged from on the state of tech M&A to chip financing to the geopolitics between America and China. Across all of those talks, the VIPs had their eyes fixed on what lies ahead—perhaps no one more so than Amanda Peterson Corio, Google’s global head of data center energy. “I live in 2031,” she told attendees. Below, some scenes from one of our favorite events of the year.

items.text:
Ask HN: What mistakes did AI make in your codebase?
In the past few weeks I've beeing working with frontier AI - Opus 5.5, Astra, Sol 6.1, Fable 5.1 and Gemini Argon.AI has become really good at coding in some sense, that's undeniable, and there are people that say you don't really need to review their code anymore.But I keep getting stuck in a sensation that's between cognitive dissonance, FOMO, and a vague sense of being gaslit, because when I review the code it writes - and this is all of them - 80% of it is right, and 20% is wrong, but in extremely subtle ways; only when you deeply understand the system and carefully review it do you spot the issues. items.text:
Show HN: 2D world SIM where each creature runs a text classifier in the browser
Each creature in this data lab is a real text classifier. You put together a workflow, and the creatures execute it. Just set a stream of incoming messages and watch them work: one filters out the spam, another tags each message's mood, finally a router sends each message to the right bin, and anything it isn't sure about goes to reviewThe classifiers run entirely in your browser. It uses a 22.7M parameter model, int8 ONNX, about 10 ms a message, no API callsOutside the lab, the creatures also evolve, chat, gossip, build huts, plot charts, count numbers, process and eat words, code and dream when asleep. items.title: Show HN: HackerBooks – HackerTube, but for books mentioned on HN
items.text:
Show HN: HackerBooks – HackerTube, but for books mentioned on HN
Saw Karpathy's HackerTube and wanted the same thing for books. So I had Claude build one (Opus 5.5).It's ~16.5k books that at least two different HN commenters brought up, from 2007 till now. Each book links back to the comments that mentioned it. Data is downloadable from the about page.To be clear: Claude wrote almost all of it, including the data pipeline and the site. I mostly steered and made calls, bought the domain name, etc.It counts mentions, so it's not perfect (praising a book and trashing it both count). If your favourite book is missing or matched to the wrong thing, tell me.

items.text:
Show HN: Sweet-search – local code search for agents (5–33% cheaper runs)
Hi everyone :)After almost a year of fighting windmills, I am proud to say I built sweet-search, a local code search tool for Claude Code, Codex and Opencode.It delivers 5-33% cheaper agentic runs with Sol 6.1 and Opus 5.5 with Claude Code, Codex and Opencode, with pooled solved tasks equal vs native (both 481 of 1,000 tasks pooled on 5 model*harness combos). Measured on 200 held-out SWE-rebench tasks. Detailed bench results are in the README.It consists of 6 tools: hybrid search with late interaction reranking, my version of grep, and others. It also has GPU accelerated indexing (for embedding and late interaction models) and low footprint incremental indexing.Some highlights: 1. items.text:
Show HN: Breath of the Wild's Hyrule digital diorama
Two weeks ago I posted a Zelda timeline here ahead of the Ocarina of Time remake. Here's what I've been working on: Breath of the Wild's Hyrule as a small 3D diorama you can explore. It has the main landmarks and a few easter eggs. It was the last Zelda game I played, early in the pandemic on a Wii U. It's been a fun little hit of nostalgia revisiting those places.The terrain information comes from data the Zelda modding community which was then smoothed and scaled down. It's Three.js with the lighting and shadows baked when the page loads.I built it with Claude, as I did the timeline. Without it, I'd never have had the time for a project this whimsical, so it wouldn't have seen the light of day. I didn't write any of the code. items.title: Show HN: BBRouter – Ben Eater's 8-bit computer, simulated on 3D breadboards
items.text:
Show HN: BBRouter – Ben Eater's 8-bit computer, simulated on 3D breadboards
Hi HN,I kept wiring Ben Eater's 8-bit computer wrong, so I built a realistic virtual breadboard editor.Some of the nice features are side-by-side diff, scope, schematics auto-sync, auto-router (BBRouter stands for breadboard router), and my favorites: upload from the real Arduino IDE and connect to your AI with MCP, let Claude & co build it or help you troubleshoot.The link is the SAP-1 running. You can orbit it, probe a hole with the scope, slow the clock down, play with the virtual displays for debugging, then you can actually build it following the step-by-step instructions.A side-goal is to create a community, there are quite a lot of simulators out there but mostly offline / too abstract to realistically use it for a real build. I also never found one that had a decent UI/UX and worke

EdgeRock-4B is based on Qwen3.5-4B, with its eight full-attention layers converted to a fixed-capacity history design that combines recurrent state, local attention, and Rock Memory Anchors (RMA) for retrieving selected distant details.

Its attention KV cache stays capped at 72

items.author: testingcatalog
items.text: EdgeRock-4B also runs locally on a laptop. On a MacBook Pro (M5 Pro, 28GB RAM) with Rock Matrix's PyTorch runtime on the Mac's GPU, it solved 17 × 23 step by step, started answering after 4.6 seconds, and generated about 9 tokens per second. https://t.co/EheFQwAy6e

items.author: testingcatalog
items.text:
Rock Matrix has open-sourced EdgeRock-4B, a small text-and-image reasoning model with fixed-capacity memory.

EdgeRock-4B keeps its attention KV cache fixed in size by holding the last 1,024 tokens in full and saving important older details to a separate bank. 

Standard language https://t.co/xwUy6EG8U1

items.title: Claude Code CHANGELOG changed
items.text: Claude Code CHANGELOG changed. New text: - Added `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_ULTRATHINK`, which turns the `ultrathink` keyword off | - Added pooled group budgets to the Claude apps gateway: one monthly budget that a group's members share, on top of each member's own limit, set with `pooled_budget` on the spend limits admin API | - Added `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_LOOPED_CROSS_CERT_DROP` to keep system cross-certificates that certify each other in a loop, for servers whose private CA needs one | - Added `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_EFFORT` to set the effort level subagents run at when nothing else names one, instead of inheriting the session's | - Added `managed.policy_mode: layered` to the Claude apps gateway: every policy that matches a developer applies, each merged over the ones listed below it, not only the first | - Added `guardrail.input_tagging` on Claude apps gateway Bedrock upstreams, which wraps prompts in the input tags that an Amazon Bedrock guardrail's prompt attacks filter needs; `all_messages_and_system` also tags the system promp

new_lines: - Added `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_ULTRATHINK`, which turns the `ultrathink` keyword off
- Added pooled group budgets to the Claude apps gateway: one monthly budget that a group's members share, on top of each member's own limit, set with `pooled_budget` on the spend limits admin API
- Added `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_LOOPED_CROSS_CERT_DROP` to keep system cross-certificates that certify each other in a loop, for servers whose private CA needs one
- Added `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_EFFORT` to set the effort level subagents run at when nothing else names one, instead of inheriting the session's
- Added `managed.policy_mode: layered` to the Claude apps gateway: every policy that matches a developer applies, each merged over the ones listed below it, not only the first

- Added `guardrail.input_tagging` on Claude apps gateway Bedrock upstreams, which wraps prompts in the input tags that an Amazon Bedrock guardrail's prompt attacks filter needs; `all_messages_and_system` also tags the system prompt
- Deprecated fast mode for Opus 4.8 as of October 30, 2026; it will be removed on November 30, 2026.
After removal, fast mode requests on Opus 4.8 return an error and do not fall back to standard Opus 4.8.
Migrate to Opus 5.5 to keep the speedup
- Fixed shell commands being left running on macOS and Linux when Claude Code exits by itself, for example when credentials are refused or a cloud session is archived
- Fixed bash aliases with line breaks in their value (except in Git Bash), and functions whose names start with a dash, being garbled or lost in the Bash tool's shell
- Fixed bash scripts started from the Bash tool stopping after their first command when `SHELLOPTS` is exported

items.title: v2.1.316
items.text:
v2.1.316
## What's changed

- Added `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_ULTRATHINK`, which turns the `ultrathink` keyword off
- Added pooled group budgets to the Claude apps gateway: one monthly budget that a group's members share, on top of each member's own limit, set with `pooled_budget` on the spend limits admin API
- Added `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_LOOPED_CROSS_CERT_DROP` to keep system cross-certificates that certify each other in a loop, for servers whose private CA needs one
- Added `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_EFFORT` to set the effort level subagents run at when nothing else names one, instead of inheriting the session's
- Added `managed.policy_mode: layered` to the Claude apps gateway: every policy that matches a developer applies, each merged over the ones listed below it, not only the first
- Added `guardrail.input_tagging` on Claude apps gateway Bedrock upstreams, which wraps prompts in the input tags that an Amazon Bedrock guardrail's prompt attacks filter needs; `all_messages_and_system` also tags the system prompt

items.author: Simon Willison
items.title: dbreunig/nesformer
items.text:
dbreunig/nesformer
dbreunig/nesformer Inspired by qwenputer by Divyansh Agrawal, Drew Breunig baked a working emulator for a Nintendo Entertainment System 6502 CPU into the weights of Qwen3.5-4B. You can now play NES ROMs such as Super Mario Bros (very slowly) running inside Qwen! In a comment on Hacker News Drew reveals the Opus 5.5 prompts he used to build this system: Read this article and any relevant source code: https://divagr.com/blog/qwenputer. Then explore if you could emulate the chip and ram in a Nintendo Entertainment System (as people do today with FPGAs in MISTRs) using this technique. If so, what size model would you have to build and if you could use smaller faster ones, could you get it to be at the standard clockspeed. Followed by: I think we should build it! Just for fun. It's okay if it's not fast. We want to be able to have the weights, and a cli to run them that we can point at a ROM. Apparently Opus found and then used this collection of conformance tests for the NES CPU released 15 years ago by Christopher Pow. Via Hacker News Tags: games, ai, generative-ai, llms, drew-breunig, qwen, conformance-suites

items.title: Childhood and Education #22: Voice Without Exit
items.text:
Childhood and Education #22: Voice Without Exit
Nikole Hannah-Jones wrote a brave self-critical piece in The New York Times, centrally about how she intentionally sent her daughter to a well-funded but failing school, PS 307, in the hopes of using voice to improve it, and how that utterly failed her daughter and failed to impact the school. Ultimately her daughter recovers, but we see a completely broken system that is unresponsive to internal voice, and until now she made no attempt to blow the whistle and utilize her professional position to do so. The whole incident illustrates not only how messed up so many of our schools are despite abundant funding, it also raises the question of what the schools are even for. If her daughter can fully recover from severe deficits and be getting As and Bs at a challenging school within a year, what are the first eight years of school for? How much of the schools, grades and tests are fake? Can we somehow do better? Table of Contents New York City PS 307. Nikole Knew And Had Exit Ramps. PS 307 Is Fraudulent And Indifferent. Moving In Unison. A Good School. What Were Elementary and Middle School Even For? The Project Was Ideological. Null Hypot

The biggest names in AI are backing a new way to opt out of scraping
OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, and Anthropic say they will adopt a new standard that publishers can use to opt out of being scraped by AI, as reported earlier by Search Engine Roundtable. With this control, publishers can apply their AI training preferences across multiple AI companies, instead of setting them individually. The shared "policy token" signal is proposed by Kevin Kelley, a technical lead for standards at Anthropic, as part of the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF). It will live within a website's robots.txt file, which has long signaled which web crawlers can and can't scrape a site - whether for search indexing, archiving, or … Read the full story at The Verge.

items.title: Ask HN: Are you putting off hardware upgrades because of AI coding tools?
items.text:
Ask HN: Are you putting off hardware upgrades because of AI coding tools?
... or has it encouraged you to upgrade?I'm still using an 8th gen i7 (w/ linux) for most of my dev work. I was going to upgrade, but now I just run like 10 terminal tabs instead of IDEs. Concurrent builds even w/ Rust and Java usually aren't a big issue. I have several backup machines so if it dies, not a big deal. If I need to, I can just tell Claude "do all builds on and iterate via CI"The benefit is for things like FastComments, I get immediate feedback if the interface is slow vs waiting for regression checks.The downside is apps like Stripe are seriously slow in FF on this machine, for some reason, despite the fact that it can play a 3d game like RDD 2 at 60fps.

Investing in any stock is kind of like gambling in the sense that you're betting your money on a company's future performance. But how do you bet on a technology that could, in the worst-case scenario, "pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity," or best case, "bring forth an age of miracles"? To some extent, Anthropic suggests in a letter at the top of its S-1 filing, you have to just believe. Anthropic's 335-page S-1 prospectus, filed Monday, is part of a steady hype escalation in Silicon Valley's interactions with Wall Street. In some ways, it's not even that bizarre; SpaceX IPO'd in June after filing an S-1 that referenced din … Read the full story at The Verge.

items.author: The Information
items.title: An Anthropic Windfall Could Await State Pension Funds
items.text:
An Anthropic Windfall Could Await State Pension Funds
Over the past year, politicians and AI executives have floated ideas for a sovereign wealth fund or other ways of giving the American public a stake in the AI boom. Some of the biggest public pension plans are poised to get a taste of the action long before those proposals come to fruition. Pension plans representing public employees in Orange County, Los Angeles, Massachusetts and South Carolina are positioned to get sizeable payouts from Anthropic’s expected initial public offering in November, thanks to the investments they made in one big Anthropic backer, Spark Capital, according to an analysis from The Information.
